digest.top_line: AREST: adjuvant RT 60Gy/30fx → 3-yr LRFS 89.2% vs 80.9% (HR 0.52, p=0.02) in resected intermediate-risk pT1-2N0 OSCC; no significant DFS/OS difference.
digest.tldr: Head-neck carried the day: phase III AREST shows adjuvant RT cuts loco-regional failure (HR 0.52) in resected intermediate-risk pT1-2N0 OSCC without a DFS/OS gain, so the RT call hinges on toxicity data not yet reported. In prostate, MROQC finds only 67.0% of high-risk M0/N0-1 pts on definitive RT intended for ≥18mo ADT.

sites.intro: MROQC: ARPI recommendations for STAMPEDE M0-eligible pts rose 0% → 23.2% post publication, and facility-level ADT variability persisted after MVA adjustment.

studies.name: MROQC ADT Practice Patterns
studies.tldr: Guideline-concordant ≥18mo ADT intended in 67.0% of high-risk M0/N0-1 pts receiving definitive RT; ARPI recommended in 23.2% of STAMPEDE-eligible pts post-publication.

details.text: 📐 MVA predictors of a guideline-concordant ADT recommendation

details: 📊 Facility-level variability persisted after MVA adjustment (P<.0001)
💊 STAMPEDE M0-eligible (27.9%): ARPI recommendations 0% pre → 23.2% post publication
🔍 Prospective MROQC statewide quality-consortium data, N=553, 26 centers, June 2020 to Nov 2024
⚠️ Intended ADT duration only; delivered duration and adherence not reported in abstract
🔗 Benchmarked against 2022 AUA/ASTRO (18-36mo ADT with RT) and STAMPEDE M0 ARPI criteria
⚠️ Abstract-only read: the full-text excerpt supplied belonged to a different paper

verdict.rationale: Practice-patterns study of intended ADT recommendations; no efficacy or outcome endpoint, so nothing here confirms or challenges SOC.
verdict.audience: Intact high-risk M0, N0-1 prostate cancer, definitive RT

studies.significance: Facility-level variability in ≥18mo ADT recommendations persisted after adjusting for cN1, grade group and PSA (P<.0001), so treating site, not only tumor features, shapes duration. Among STAMPEDE M0-eligible pts, ARPI recommendations reached only 23.2% after publication, a gap a department can audit directly in its own high-risk RT cohort.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective **statewide quality-consortium** data (MROQC), **N=553** across **26 centers**, June 2020 to November 2024. Multivariable analysis of predictors, a mixed-effects model with treatment site as random intercept, and ARPI adoption compared before vs after STAMPEDE M0 publication.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Intact **high-risk M0, N0-1** prostate cancer treated with definitive RT: cT3/4 13.3%, **cN1 19.9%**, **GG 4-5 75.0%**, PSA ≥20 ng/mL 40.0%. **27.9%** met STAMPEDE M0 criteria (≥2 of cT3/T4, GG 4-5, PSA ≥40 ng/mL, or cN1).

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** intended guideline-concordant ADT (**GC-ADT, ≥18 months**) per 2022 AUA/ASTRO. Also assessed: ARPI recommendation in STAMPEDE-eligible pts and facility-level variability.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **91.3%** recommended any ADT, **67.0%** guideline-concordant. ARPI recommendations in STAMPEDE-eligible pts rose from **0% to 23.2%** after publication; facility variability persisted on MVA (**P<.0001**).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intact high-risk M0/N0-1 prostate cancer treated with definitive RT. Does not represent post-prostatectomy, intermediate-risk, or metastatic pts, or the ADT duration actually delivered.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Benchmarks practice against the **2022 AUA/ASTRO** 18-36 month recommendation and **STAMPEDE M0** ARPI intensification criteria. Single-state data, and the source offers no comparison with other practice settings.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The abstract gives **no reasons for sub-18mo recommendations** (comorbidity, pt preference, toxicity), so non-concordance is not necessarily poor care. The ARPI comparison is an **uncontrolled before-after** design, and no OR is reported for cT3/4.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The strongest predictors of a concordant recommendation were **grade group** (GG5 OR 9.45) and cN1, consistent with shorter courses being offered when high-risk status rests on other features. **Residual site variability** points to local norms beyond the modelled case mix, though unmeasured covariates could contribute.

studies.interpretation:
The headline figure, two thirds of high-risk pts recommended at least 18 months of ADT with definitive RT, reads easily as a quality failure. The abstract supports that reading less than it first appears to. The endpoint is intended duration at the time of RT, a recommendation rather than a delivered course, and the reasons behind a shorter recommendation are not reported. Long-course ADT in older men carries real cardiometabolic, skeletal and fatigue costs, and part of the non-concordance in any registry will be deliberate: comorbidity, competing mortality, or a pt who declines after an informed discussion. A dataset that cannot separate those decisions from habit measures the upper bound of the quality gap, not its true size.

The multivariable pattern tells you more. Grade group 5 (OR 9.45), grade group 4 (OR 6.23), PSA ≥40 ng/mL (OR 3.64) and cN1 (OR 2.94) were each tied to a concordant recommendation. The likely corollary is that pts whose high-risk status rests on PSA below the ≥40 threshold or on T-stage, with lower grade, are the ones most often offered shorter courses. That matches how many radiation oncologists treat high-risk as a mixed category in which grade dominates, while the guideline benchmark used here makes no such distinction. The abstract reports no estimate for cT3/4, and the reference categories are not stated, so how much T-stage alone moves the recommendation cannot be judged from the source.

The persisting facility-level variability (P<.0001) is the finding with the most operational weight. A mixed-effects model with site as a random intercept suits the question, and the result says that where a pt is treated predicts the recommendation beyond the case-mix variables in the model. The usual caveat applies: unmeasured case mix, such as comorbidity burden or referral patterns, can look like a site effect, and the abstract does not list the full covariate set.

The ARPI result is the sharper practice signal. STAMPEDE M0 defined an intensification population, and 27.9% of this cohort met its criteria. Recommendations rose from 0% before publication to 23.2% after. A zero baseline is expected because the data did not yet exist, so the comparison documents adoption rather than departure from an established standard. Uptake below a quarter could reflect access and cost, reluctance to extrapolate from a trial enrolled under older staging, or uncertainty about how modern imaging interacts with the eligibility criteria. The source tests none of these explanations.

What the study leaves open is whether any of this changes outcomes. It does not follow pts, report delivered duration, or link concordance to biochemical or metastatic endpoints. Its use is as a benchmark: a department can set its own high-risk RT cohort against 67.0% concordance and 23.2% eligible ARPI uptake, then ask whether its non-concordant cases are documented decisions or defaults.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Grade group drove concordant ADT recommendations most (GG5 OR 9.45, GG4 OR 6.23), and site-level variability survived adjustment (P<.0001). For an RT department the benchmark is concrete: 67.0% intended ≥18mo ADT and 23.2% ARPI uptake in STAMPEDE M0-eligible pts after publication.

open_questions: Delivered vs intended ADT duration in routine definitive RT practice
Drivers of facility-level variation in ADT duration recommendations
Barriers to ARPI intensification in STAMPEDE M0-eligible pts

sites.intro: AREST informs adjuvant RT addition for pN0 OSCC with DOI 5-10mm, PNI, LVE, or poor differentiation: loco-regional gain, no survival gain, RT morbidity unquantified.

studies.name: AREST
studies.tldr: 3-yr LRFS 89.2% vs 80.9% (HR 0.52, p=0.02) with adjuvant RT vs observation in resected intermediate-risk pT1-2N0 OSCC; no significant DFS/OS difference.
details: 🔍 Multicenter open-label phase III RCT from India, 1:1, N=392 (191 RT vs 201 observation)
🔍 RT: 60Gy/30fx over 6 wks to resected tumor bed + at-risk neck nodal region

subdetails: At least ipsilateral level I-III neck dissection with ≥16 nodes
≥1 intermediate risk factor: DOI ≥5 to ≤10mm, PNI, LVE, or poor differentiation

details.text: 📊 Loco-regional endpoints, adjuvant RT vs observation

details: 📊 DFS and OS not significantly different; no survival HRs reported in source
⚠️ Oral tongue > buccal mucosa benefit is an exploratory subgroup; no subgroup HR in source
⚠️ Control arm 3-yr LRFS 80.9% vs 70% assumed in the power calculation
⚠️ No RT toxicity or salvage data in abstract; morbidity trade-off unquantified

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase III hit LRFS primary at 47.2 mo median f/u; DFS/OS not significantly different and no toxicity data in abstract, so supports rather than mandates adjuvant RT.
verdict.audience: Resected pT1-2N0 OSCC, margins ≥5mm, ≥1 intermediate-risk feature

studies.significance: Competing-risk LRF incidence was 10.6% vs 18.9% (HR 0.52) with 60Gy/30fx to tumor bed and at-risk neck. Controls had ≥5mm margins and a level I-III dissection with ≥16 nodes, so this is RT's increment over high-quality surgery alone. It moves adjuvant RT vs observation most for oral tongue, an exploratory subgroup.
studies.monday_clinic: In pT1-2N0 OSCC resected with ≥5mm margins and an adequate level I-III neck dissection but carrying PNI, LVE, poor differentiation or DOI ≥5 to ≤10mm, this supports discussing adjuvant RT for loco-regional control; it does not extend to close-margin, limited-neck or node-positive disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Multicenter, open-label, phase III RCT** from India, 1:1, stratified by oral cavity subsite, PNI/LVE and differentiation. **N=392** (191 RT, 201 observation); median follow-up **47.2 mo** (IQR 30-59.4). Powered at 80% to detect HR 0.6256, assuming 3-yr LRFS 70% with observation.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **pT1-T2, pN0 OSCC** after adequate surgery: **clear margins ≥5mm** and at least ipsilateral level I-III neck dissection with **≥16 nodes**. Required **≥1 intermediate risk factor**: DOI ≥5 to ≤10mm, PNI, LVE, or poor differentiation.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **60Gy in 30 fractions over 6 weeks** to the resected tumor bed and at-risk neck nodal region. Technique and nodal volume definitions not stated in source; no concurrent systemic therapy described.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** loco-regional recurrence-free survival, from randomization to first local and/or regional recurrence. Also reported: cumulative incidence of loco-regional failure with death as competing event, DFS, OS.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **LRFS benefit held on PP and competing-risk analyses**; **DFS and OS not significantly different**, with no survival HRs in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The abstract describes the evidence for adjuvant RT in this setting as **largely retrospective**; AREST is the randomised test of that practice. The RTOG and EORTC postoperative trials tested adding concurrent chemo to RT in high-risk resected disease and did not randomise RT itself against observation.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pT1-2N0 OSCC with margins ≥5mm, an ipsilateral level I-III neck dissection yielding ≥16 nodes, and ≥1 intermediate-risk feature. Does not represent close or positive margins, pN+ disease, or pts without a formal neck dissection.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Control arm beat its design assumption** (3-yr LRFS 80.9% vs 70% assumed), so the absolute gain sits against a lower-risk baseline than planned. **Oral tongue vs buccal mucosa** is an exploratory subgroup with no HR in source, and no result is given per risk factor. Salvage treatment at recurrence is not described, which bears on the OS read.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Loco-regional control improved **without DFS or OS separation**; one explanation is effective salvage of isolated recurrences in observed pts, which the abstract cannot confirm. The decision it moves is **adjuvant RT vs observation** after adequate resection, weighed against RT morbidity the abstract does not report.

studies.interpretation:
AREST gives a randomised answer to a question head and neck teams have mostly settled on retrospective series: whether a cleanly resected, pathologically node-negative early oral cavity primary earns adjuvant RT because it carries perineural invasion, lymphovascular emboli, poor differentiation, or an intermediate depth of invasion. On the prespecified endpoint the answer is yes. The ITT hazard ratio of 0.52 is echoed by the per-protocol estimate of 0.43 and by the competing-risk analysis, which answers the usual objection that a Kaplan-Meier recurrence endpoint can flatter an arm when deaths without recurrence are censored. The observed effect was also larger than the hazard ratio of 0.6256 the trial was powered to detect, although an upper confidence bound of 0.91 still admits a modest benefit.

The design feature that matters most for transfer is the surgical floor. Every pt had margins of at least 5mm and at least an ipsilateral level I-III neck dissection with 16 or more nodes, so the pN0 label is reliable and the observation arm was not a proxy for undertreatment. What RT added is an increment over good surgery, not a repair of inadequate surgery. The same feature limits extrapolation: a pt with a close margin, a limited neck dissection, or a low nodal yield sits outside the trial, and the tempting inference that such pts would benefit more is plausible but untested here. The observation arm also did better than planned, with 3-yr LRFS of 80.9% against an assumed 70%, so the absolute gain a reader weighs against RT morbidity is set against a lower-risk baseline than the protocol anticipated.

DFS and OS were not significantly different, and two readings compete. The trial was powered for loco-regional control, not survival, so a smaller survival effect could be missed. Alternatively, isolated loco-regional recurrence in the observed arm may often be salvaged, which turns the choice into a trade between up-front RT for everyone and salvage treatment for the minority who recur. The abstract reports neither salvage rates nor salvage morbidity, so these cannot be separated, and that gap is where the decision actually lives. Six weeks of RT to the oral cavity and neck carries late effects this abstract does not quantify, so the balance of benefit and harm cannot yet be read from the report.

Three further points temper application. The oral tongue versus buccal mucosa difference is labelled exploratory, and no subgroup hazard ratio or interaction test appears in the source; stratification by subsite makes the comparison fairer but it remains hypothesis-generating. No result is given by individual risk factor, so whether intermediate depth of invasion alone justifies RT as much as perineural invasion does is unanswered. The target was the tumor bed plus the at-risk neck, so the trial cannot say whether a primary-bed-only volume would capture most of the gain.

Taken together this is a confirmatory randomised read. It moves adjuvant RT for intermediate-risk pT1-2N0 OSCC from retrospective justification to randomised support for loco-regional control, without showing that pts live longer. The full publication needs to supply toxicity, salvage outcomes and per-factor results before the benefit-harm balance can be stated for an individual pt.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Competing-risk LRF incidence 10.6% vs 18.9% (HR 0.52) with 60Gy/30fx to tumor bed and at-risk neck, after surgery that already met ≥5mm margins and ≥16 nodes. It moves adjuvant RT vs observation in pT1-2N0 OSCC, strongest for oral tongue in an exploratory subgroup; smaller target volumes untested.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Benefit was measured against surgery with clear margins ≥5mm and an ipsilateral level I-III dissection yielding ≥16 nodes, so RT added loco-regional control even after high-quality resection. Pathology reporting of PNI, LVE, differentiation and DOI now gates the adjuvant referral; the data do not cover close margins or a limited neck.

open_questions: Which intermediate-risk feature (PNI, LVE, DOI, grade) drives the benefit?
Does the oral tongue benefit hold as a prespecified subgroup?
Late RT toxicity and salvage outcomes in the observation arm

papers.title: Androgen Deprivation Therapy Practice Patterns in High-Risk Prostate Cancer Treated With Definitive Radiotherapy: Prospective Results From a Statewide Quality Consortium
papers.abstract: PURPOSE The 2022 AUA/ASTRO guidelines recommend 18-36 months of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) with definitive radiotherapy for localized, high-risk prostate cancer. The STAMPEDE M0 trial supports intensification with androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) for patients with ≥2 cT3/T4, Grade Group [GG] 4-5, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) ≥40 ng/mL, or cN1. Given advances in imaging, risk stratification, and treatment delivery, we characterized contemporary practice patterns using prospective data from the Michigan Radiation Oncology Quality Consortium (MROQC). METHODS Patients enrolled in MROQC with intact, high-risk M0/N0-1 prostate cancer were included. Clinical information, including intended ADT duration and ARPI use, was prospectively collected. The primary outcome was intended guideline-concordant ADT (GC-ADT, ≥18 months). Multivariable analyses (MVA) assessed associations between clinical factors and GC-ADT recommendations. We compared the adoption of ARPI with standard therapies before and after the publication of STAMPEDE M0. Facility-level variability was evaluated using a mixed-effects model, with the treatment site as a random intercept. RESULTS Between June 2020 and November 2024, 553 patients across 26 centers were included: cT3/4 (13.3%), cN1 (19.9%), GG 4-5 (75.0%), and PSA ≥20 ng/mL (40.0%). Overall, 91.3% were recommended ADT, with 67.0% being guideline-concordant. On MVA, GC-ADT was significantly associated with cN1 (odds ratio [OR], 2.94 [95% CI, 1.44 to 5.99]), GG (GG4 OR, 6.23 [95% CI, 2.85 to 13.62]; GG5 OR, 9.45 [95% CI, 4.46 to 20.06]), and PSA ≥40 (OR, 3.64 [95% CI, 1.22–10.87]). Facility-level variability persisted in the MVA ( P < .0001). Among the 27.9% who met meeting STAMPEDE criteria, ARPI recommendations increased from 0% prepublication to 23.2% afterward. CONCLUSION Within a statewide quality consortium, guideline-concordant ADT recommendations occurred in two thirds of patients, with ARPI intensification in under 25% among STAMPEDE-eligible patients. These findings highlight the need for individualized ADT strategies and collaborative efforts to standardize high-quality care.

papers.title: Adjuvant radiotherapy versus observation following curative surgery for early-stage oral squamous cell carcinoma (AREST; CTRI/2017/07/009114).
authors: AREST Study - Head and Neck Cooperative Oncology Group
papers.abstract: 6000 Background: The role of adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) in early-stage, node-negative oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) with one or more intermediate risk factors - such as depth of invasion (DOI) ≥5 to ≤10mm, perineural invasion (PNI), lymphovascular emboli (LVE), or poor differentiation - remains debatable and is largely based on retrospective data. This multicenter, open-label, phase III randomized controlled trial was designed to assess the impact of post-operative adjuvant RT in this setting. Methods: Patients with early-stage (pT1-T2), node-negative (pN0) OSCC undergoing adequate surgery (defined as clear margins ≥5mm and at least ipsilateral level I-III neck dissection with ≥16 nodes) with presence of one or more intermediate risk factors were screened. Eligible patients underwent stratified randomization (oral cavity subsite, PNI/LVE, and differentiation) in 1:1 ratio to either observation or adjuvant RT (60Gy in 30 fractions over 6-weeks) to the resected tumor-bed and at-risk neck nodal region after written informed consent. Primary endpoint was loco-regional recurrence-free survival (LRFS) measured from randomization to first documented event of local and/or regional recurrence from index cancer. All time-to-event outcomes were computed using Kaplan-Meier (KM) method with log-rank test for comparison and expressed as 3-year point estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The planned sample size (N=392) provided 80% power at an α of 0.05 to detect a Hazard Ratio (HR) of 0.6256, assuming 3-year LRFS of 70% in the observation arm. Results: Following curative surgery, a total of 392 patients were randomized (191 to adjuvant RT; 201 to observation). Baseline characteristics were balanced between the two arms. At a median follow-up of 47.2 months (inter-quartile range=30-59.4 months), 3-year KM estimate of LRFS was 89.2% in adjuvant RT arm vs 80.9% in observation arm (HR=0.52, 95%CI=0.30-0.91; p=0.02) in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population and 91.1% vs 80.9% (HR=0.43, 95%CI=0.23-0.80; p=0.01) on per-protocol (PP) analyses. Cumulative incidence of loco-regional failure with death as competing event was 10.6% (95%CI=6.1%-15.1%) with adjuvant RT and 18.9% (95%CI=13.3%-24.6%) with observation (HR=0.52, 95%CI=0.30-0.91; p=0.021) in the ITT population and 8.7% (95%CI=4.3%-13.1%) vs 18.9% (95%CI=13.3%-24.6%) (HR=0.43, 95%CI=0.23-0.79; p=0.007) on PP analyses. Disease-free and overall survival were not significantly different between the two arms. Subgroup analysis identified oral tongue deriving higher benefit of adjuvant RT compared to buccal mucosa. Conclusions: Adjuvant RT significantly reduces risk of loco-regional recurrence for early-stage, node-negative adequately resected OSCC, particularly oral tongue. However, such reduction in loco-regional failure does not translate into significant survival benefit. Clinical trial information: CTRI/2017/07/009114.
